Such code runs prior to general startup code that initializes <font SIZE="-1">RAM</font> and calls constructors, but after the bit of startup code from AVR-LibC that sets <tt>&quot;EIND&quot;</tt> to the segment where the vector table is located. 

 <pre> #include &lt;avr/io.h&gt;
 
 static void
 __attribute__((section(&quot;.init3&quot;),naked,used,no_instrument_function))
 init3_set_eind (void)
 {
 __asm volatile (&quot;ldi r24,pm_hh8(__trampolines_start)\n\t&quot;
 &quot;out %i0,r24&quot; :: &quot;n&quot; (&amp;EIND) : &quot;r24&quot;,&quot;memory&quot;);
 }</pre>The <tt>&quot;__trampolines_start&quot;</tt> symbol is defined in the linker script.
<dt>*
<dd>Stubs are generated automatically by the linker if the following two conditions are met:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>-&lt;The address of a label is taken by means of the &quot;gs&quot; modifier&gt;
<dd>(short for <i>generate stubs</i>) like so: 

 <pre> LDI r24, lo8(gs(&lt;func&gt;))
 LDI r25, hi8(gs(&lt;func&gt;))</pre><dt>-&lt;The final location of that label is in a code segment&gt;
<dd><i>outside</i> the segment where the stubs are located.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt>*
<dd>The compiler emits such <tt>&quot;gs&quot;</tt> modifiers for code labels in the following situations:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>-&lt;Taking address of a function or code label.&gt;
<dd><dt>-&lt;Computed goto.&gt;
<dd><dt>-&lt;If prologue-save function is used, see <b>-mcall-prologues</b>&gt;
<dd>command-line option.
<dt>-&lt;Switch/case dispatch tables. If you do not want such dispatch&gt;
<dd>tables you can specify the <b>-fno-jump-tables</b> command-line option.
<dt>-&lt;C and C<font SIZE="-2">++</font> constructors/destructors called during startup/shutdown.&gt;
<dd><dt>-&lt;If the tools hit a &quot;gs()&quot; modifier explained above.&gt;
<dd></dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt>*
<dd>Jumping to non-symbolic addresses like so is <i>not</i> supported: 

 <pre> int main (void)
 {
 /* Call function at word address 0x2 */
 return ((int(*)(void)) 0x2)();
 }</pre>Instead, a stub has to be set up, i.e. the function has to be called through a symbol (<tt>&quot;func_4&quot;</tt> in the example): 

 <pre> int main (void)
 {
 extern int func_4 (void);
 
 /* Call function at byte address 0x4 */
 return func_4();
 }</pre>and the application be linked with <b>-Wl,--defsym,func_4=0x4</b>. Alternatively, <tt>&quot;func_4&quot;</tt> can be defined in the linker script.</dl>
 

 Handling of the <tt>&quot;RAMPD&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPX&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPY&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> Special Function Registers 

 Some <font SIZE="-1">AVR</font> devices support memories larger than the 64 KiB range that can be accessed with 16-bit pointers. To access memory locations outside this 64 KiB range, the content of a <tt>&quot;RAMP&quot;</tt> register is used as high part of the address: The <tt>&quot;X&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;Y&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;Z&quot;</tt> address register is concatenated with the <tt>&quot;RAMPX&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPY&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> special function register, respectively, to get a wide address. Similarly, <tt>&quot;RAMPD&quot;</tt> is used together with direct addressing.
<dl COMPACT><dt>*
<dd>The startup code initializes the <tt>&quot;RAMP&quot;</tt> special function registers with zero.
<dt>*
<dd>If a <font SIZE="-1"><b>AVR</b></font><b> Named Address Spaces,named address space</b> other than generic or <tt>&quot;__flash&quot;</tt> is used, then <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> is set as needed before the operation.
<dt>*
<dd>If the device supports <font SIZE="-1">RAM</font> larger than 64 KiB and the compiler needs to change <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> to accomplish an operation, <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> is reset to zero after the operation.
<dt>*
<dd>If the device comes with a specific <tt>&quot;RAMP&quot;</tt> register, the <font SIZE="-1">ISR</font> prologue/epilogue saves/restores that <font SIZE="-1">SFR</font> and initializes it with zero in case the <font SIZE="-1">ISR</font> code might (implicitly) use it.
<dt>*
<dd><font SIZE="-1">RAM</font> larger than 64 KiB is not supported by <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> for <font SIZE="-1">AVR</font> targets. If you use inline assembler to read from locations outside the 16-bit address range and change one of the <tt>&quot;RAMP&quot;</tt> registers, you must reset it to zero after the access.</dl>
 

 <font SIZE="-1">AVR</font> Built-in Macros 

 <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> defines several built-in macros so that the user code can test for the presence or absence of features. Almost any of the following built-in macros are deduced from device capabilities and thus triggered by the <b>-mmcu=</b> command-line option. 

 For even more AVR-specific built-in macros see <font SIZE="-1"><b>AVR</b></font><b> Named Address Spaces</b> and <font SIZE="-1"><b>AVR</b></font><b> Built-in Functions</b>.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&quot;__AVR_ARCH__&quot;
<dd>Build-in macro that resolves to a decimal number that identifies the architecture and depends on the <b>-mmcu=</b><i>mcu</i> option. Possible values are: 

 <tt>2</tt>, <tt>25</tt>, <tt>3</tt>, <tt>31</tt>, <tt>35</tt>, <tt>4</tt>, <tt>5</tt>, <tt>51</tt>, <tt>6</tt> 

 for <i>mcu</i>=<tt>&quot;avr2&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr25&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr3&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr31&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr35&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr4&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr5&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr51&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avr6&quot;</tt>, 

 respectively and 

 <tt>100</tt>, <tt>102</tt>, <tt>103</tt>, <tt>104</tt>, <tt>105</tt>, <tt>106</tt>, <tt>107</tt> 

 for <i>mcu</i>=<tt>&quot;avrtiny&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega2&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega3&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega4&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega5&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega6&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;avrxmega7&quot;</tt>, respectively. If <i>mcu</i> specifies a device, this built-in macro is set accordingly. For example, with <b>-mmcu=atmega8</b> the macro is defined to <tt>4</tt>.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_<i>Device</i>__&quot;
<dd>Setting <b>-mmcu=</b><i>device</i> defines this built-in macro which reflects the device's name. For example, <b>-mmcu=atmega8</b> defines the built-in macro <tt>&quot;__AVR_ATmega8__&quot;</tt>, <b>-mmcu=attiny261a</b> defines <tt>&quot;__AVR_ATtiny261A__&quot;</tt>, etc. 

 The built-in macros' names follow the scheme <tt>&quot;__AVR_</tt>Device<tt>__&quot;</tt> where <i>Device</i> is the device name as from the <font SIZE="-1">AVR</font> user manual. The difference between <i>Device</i> in the built-in macro and <i>device</i> in <b>-mmcu=</b><i>device</i> is that the latter is always lowercase. 

 If <i>device</i> is not a device but only a core architecture like <b>avr51</b>, this macro is not defined.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_DEVICE_NAME__&quot;
<dd>Setting <b>-mmcu=</b><i>device</i> defines this built-in macro to the device's name. For example, with <b>-mmcu=atmega8</b> the macro is defined to <tt>&quot;atmega8&quot;</tt>. 

 If <i>device</i> is not a device but only a core architecture like <b>avr51</b>, this macro is not defined.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_XMEGA__&quot;
<dd>The device / architecture belongs to the <font SIZE="-1">XMEGA</font> family of devices.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_ELPM__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;ELPM&quot;</tt> instruction.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_ELPMX__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;ELPM R</tt>n<tt>,Z&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;ELPM R</tt>n<tt>,Z+&quot;</tt> instructions.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_MOVW__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;MOVW&quot;</tt> instruction to perform 16-bit register-register moves.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_LPMX__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;LPM R</tt>n<tt>,Z&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;LPM R</tt>n<tt>,Z+&quot;</tt> instructions.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_MUL__&quot;
<dd>The device has a hardware multiplier.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_JMP_CALL__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;JMP&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;CALL&quot;</tt> instructions. This is the case for devices with more than 8 KiB of program memory.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_EIJMP_EICALL__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_3_BYTE_PC__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;EIJMP&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;EICALL&quot;</tt> instructions. This is the case for devices with more than 128 KiB of program memory. This also means that the program counter (<font SIZE="-1">PC</font>) is 3 bytes wide.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_2_BYTE_PC__&quot;
<dd>The program counter (<font SIZE="-1">PC</font>) is 2 bytes wide. This is the case for devices with up to 128 KiB of program memory.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_8BIT_SP__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_16BIT_SP__&quot;
<dd>The stack pointer (<font SIZE="-1">SP</font>) register is treated as 8-bit respectively 16-bit register by the compiler. The definition of these macros is affected by <b>-mtiny-stack</b>.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_SPH__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_SP8__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <font SIZE="-1">SPH</font> (high part of stack pointer) special function register or has an 8-bit stack pointer, respectively. The definition of these macros is affected by <b>-mmcu=</b> and in the cases of <b>-mmcu=avr2</b> and <b>-mmcu=avr25</b> also by <b>-msp8</b>.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_RAMPD__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_RAMPX__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_RAMPY__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_RAMPZ__&quot;
<dd>The device has the <tt>&quot;RAMPD&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPX&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPY&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RAMPZ&quot;</tt> special function register, respectively.
<dt>&quot;__NO_INTERRUPTS__&quot;
<dd>This macro reflects the <b>-mno-interrupts</b> command-line option.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_ERRATA_SKIP__&quot;
<dd><dt>&quot;__AVR_ERRATA_SKIP_JMP_CALL__&quot;
<dd>Some <font SIZE="-1">AVR</font> devices (<font SIZE="-1">AT90S8515,</font> ATmega103) must not skip 32-bit instructions because of a hardware erratum. Skip instructions are <tt>&quot;SBRS&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SBRC&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SBIS&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SBIC&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;CPSE&quot;</tt>. The second macro is only defined if <tt>&quot;__AVR_HAVE_JMP_CALL__&quot;</tt> is also set.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_ISA_RMW__&quot;
<dd>The device has Read-Modify-Write instructions (<font SIZE="-1">XCH, LAC, LAS</font> and <font SIZE="-1">LAT</font>).
<dt>&quot;__AVR_SFR_OFFSET__=<i>offset</i>&quot;
<dd>Instructions that can address I/O special function registers directly like <tt>&quot;IN&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;OUT&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SBI&quot;</tt>, etc. may use a different address as if addressed by an instruction to access <font SIZE="-1">RAM</font> like <tt>&quot;LD&quot;</tt> or <tt>&quot;STS&quot;</tt>. This offset depends on the device architecture and has to be subtracted from the <font SIZE="-1">RAM</font> address in order to get the respective I/O address.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_SHORT_CALLS__&quot;
<dd>The <b>-mshort-calls</b> command line option is set.
<dt>&quot;__AVR_PM_BASE_ADDRESS__=<i>addr</i>&quot;
<dd>Some devices support reading from flash memory by means of <tt>&quot;LD*&quot;</tt> instructions. The flash memory is seen in the data address space at an offset of <tt>&quot;__AVR_PM_BASE_ADDRESS__&quot;</tt>. If this macro is not defined, this feature is not available. If defined, the address space is linear and there is no need to put <tt>&quot;.rodata&quot;</tt> into <font SIZE="-1">RAM.</font> This is handled by the default linker description file, and is currently available for <tt>&quot;avrtiny&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;avrxmega3&quot;</tt>. Even more convenient, there is no need to use address spaces like <tt>&quot;__flash&quot;</tt> or features like attribute <tt>&quot;progmem&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;pgm_read_*&quot;</tt>.
<dt>&quot;__WITH_AVRLIBC__&quot;
<dd>The compiler is configured to be used together with AVR-Libc. See the <b>--with-avrlibc</b> configure option.</dl>
 

 <i>Blackfin Options</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mcpu=</b><i>cpu</i>[<b>-</b><i>sirevision</i>]
<dd>Specifies the name of the target Blackfin processor. Currently, <i>cpu</i> can be one of <b>bf512</b>, <b>bf514</b>, <b>bf516</b>, <b>bf518</b>, <b>bf522</b>, <b>bf523</b>, <b>bf524</b>, <b>bf525</b>, <b>bf526</b>, <b>bf527</b>, <b>bf531</b>, <b>bf532</b>, <b>bf533</b>, <b>bf534</b>, <b>bf536</b>, <b>bf537</b>, <b>bf538</b>, <b>bf539</b>, <b>bf542</b>, <b>bf544</b>, <b>bf547</b>, <b>bf548</b>, <b>bf549</b>, <b>bf542m</b>, <b>bf544m</b>, <b>bf547m</b>, <b>bf548m</b>, <b>bf549m</b>, <b>bf561</b>, <b>bf592</b>. 

 The optional <i>sirevision</i> specifies the silicon revision of the target Blackfin processor. Any workarounds available for the targeted silicon revision are enabled. If <i>sirevision</i> is <b>none</b>, no workarounds are enabled. If <i>sirevision</i> is <b>any</b>, all workarounds for the targeted processor are enabled. The <tt>&quot;__SILICON_REVISION__&quot;</tt> macro is defined to two hexadecimal digits representing the major and minor numbers in the silicon revision. If <i>sirevision</i> is <b>none</b>, the <tt>&quot;__SILICON_REVISION__&quot;</tt> is not defined. If <i>sirevision</i> is <b>any</b>, the <tt>&quot;__SILICON_REVISION__&quot;</tt> is defined to be <tt>0xffff</tt>. If this optional <i>sirevision</i> is not used, <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> assumes the latest known silicon revision of the targeted Blackfin processor. 

 <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> defines a preprocessor macro for the specified <i>cpu</i>. For the <b>bfin-elf</b> toolchain, this option causes the hardware <font SIZE="-1">BSP</font> provided by libgloss to be linked in if <b>-msim</b> is not given. 

 Without this option, <b>bf532</b> is used as the processor by default. 

 Note that support for <b>bf561</b> is incomplete. For <b>bf561</b>, only the preprocessor macro is defined.
<dt><b>-msim</b>
<dd>Specifies that the program will be run on the simulator. This causes the simulator <font SIZE="-1">BSP</font> provided by libgloss to be linked in. This option has effect only for <b>bfin-elf</b> toolchain. Certain other options, such as <b>-mid-shared-library</b> and <b>-mfdpic</b>, imply <b>-msim</b>.
<dt><b>-momit-leaf-frame-pointer</b>
<dd>Don't keep the frame pointer in a register for leaf functions. This avoids the instructions to save, set up and restore frame pointers and makes an extra register available in leaf functions.
<dt><b>-mspecld-anomaly</b>
<dd>When enabled, the compiler ensures that the generated code does not contain speculative loads after jump instructions. If this option is used, <tt>&quot;__WORKAROUND_SPECULATIVE_LOADS&quot;</tt> is defined.
<dt><b>-mno-specld-anomaly</b>
<dd>Don't generate extra code to prevent speculative loads from occurring.
<dt><b>-mcsync-anomaly</b>
<dd>When enabled, the compiler ensures that the generated code does not contain <font SIZE="-1">CSYNC</font> or <font SIZE="-1">SSYNC</font> instructions too soon after conditional branches. If this option is used, <tt>&quot;__WORKAROUND_SPECULATIVE_SYNCS&quot;</tt> is defined.
<dt><b>-mno-csync-anomaly</b>
<dd>Don't generate extra code to prevent <font SIZE="-1">CSYNC</font> or <font SIZE="-1">SSYNC</font> instructions from occurring too soon after a conditional branch.
<dt><b>-mlow64k</b>
<dd>When enabled, the compiler is free to take advantage of the knowledge that the entire program fits into the low 64k of memory.
<dt><b>-mno-low64k</b>
<dd>Assume that the program is arbitrarily large. This is the default.
<dt><b>-mstack-check-l1</b>
<dd>Do stack checking using information placed into L1 scratchpad memory by the uClinux kernel.
<dt><b>-mid-shared-library</b>
<dd>Generate code that supports shared libraries via the library <font SIZE="-1">ID</font> method. This allows for execute in place and shared libraries in an environment without virtual memory management. This option implies <b>-fPIC</b>. With a <b>bfin-elf</b> target, this option implies <b>-msim</b>.
<dt><b>-mno-id-shared-library</b>
<dd>Generate code that doesn't assume ID-based shared libraries are being used. This is the default.
<dt><b>-mleaf-id-shared-library</b>
<dd>Generate code that supports shared libraries via the library <font SIZE="-1">ID</font> method, but assumes that this library or executable won't link against any other <font SIZE="-1">ID</font> shared libraries. That allows the compiler to use faster code for jumps and calls.
<dt><b>-mno-leaf-id-shared-library</b>
<dd>Do not assume that the code being compiled won't link against any <font SIZE="-1">ID</font> shared libraries. Slower code is generated for jump and call insns.
<dt><b>-mshared-library-id=n</b>
<dd>Specifies the identification number of the ID-based shared library being compiled. Specifying a value of 0 generates more compact code; specifying other values forces the allocation of that number to the current library but is no more space- or time-efficient than omitting this option.
<dt><b>-msep-data</b>
<dd>Generate code that allows the data segment to be located in a different area of memory from the text segment. This allows for execute in place in an environment without virtual memory management by eliminating relocations against the text section.
<dt><b>-mno-sep-data</b>
<dd>Generate code that assumes that the data segment follows the text segment. This is the default.
<dt><b>-mlong-calls</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-long-calls</b>
<dd>Tells the compiler to perform function calls by first loading the address of the function into a register and then performing a subroutine call on this register. This switch is needed if the target function lies outside of the 24-bit addressing range of the offset-based version of subroutine call instruction. 

 This feature is not enabled by default. Specifying <b>-mno-long-calls</b> restores the default behavior. Note these switches have no effect on how the compiler generates code to handle function calls via function pointers.
<dt><b>-mfast-fp</b>
<dd>Link with the fast floating-point library. This library relaxes some of the <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> floating-point standard's rules for checking inputs against Not-a-Number (<font SIZE="-1">NAN</font>), in the interest of performance.
<dt><b>-minline-plt</b>
<dd>Enable inlining of <font SIZE="-1">PLT</font> entries in function calls to functions that are not known to bind locally. It has no effect without <b>-mfdpic</b>.
<dt><b>-mmulticore</b>
<dd>Build a standalone application for multicore Blackfin processors. This option causes proper start files and link scripts supporting multicore to be used, and defines the macro <tt>&quot;__BFIN_MULTICORE&quot;</tt>. It can only be used with <b>-mcpu=bf561</b>[<b>-</b><i>sirevision</i>]. 

 This option can be used with <b>-mcorea</b> or <b>-mcoreb</b>, which selects the one-application-per-core programming model. Without <b>-mcorea</b> or <b>-mcoreb</b>, the single-application/dual-core programming model is used. In this model, the main function of Core B should be named as <tt>&quot;coreb_main&quot;</tt>. 

 If this option is not used, the single-core application programming model is used.
<dt><b>-mcorea</b>
<dd>Build a standalone application for Core A of <font SIZE="-1">BF561</font> when using the one-application-per-core programming model. Proper start files and link scripts are used to support Core A, and the macro <tt>&quot;__BFIN_COREA&quot;</tt> is defined. This option can only be used in conjunction with <b>-mmulticore</b>.
<dt><b>-mcoreb</b>
<dd>Build a standalone application for Core B of <font SIZE="-1">BF561</font> when using the one-application-per-core programming model. Proper start files and link scripts are used to support Core B, and the macro <tt>&quot;__BFIN_COREB&quot;</tt> is defined. When this option is used, <tt>&quot;coreb_main&quot;</tt> should be used instead of <tt>&quot;main&quot;</tt>. This option can only be used in conjunction with <b>-mmulticore</b>.
<dt><b>-msdram</b>
<dd>Build a standalone application for <font SIZE="-1">SDRAM.</font> Proper start files and link scripts are used to put the application into <font SIZE="-1">SDRAM,</font> and the macro <tt>&quot;__BFIN_SDRAM&quot;</tt> is defined. The loader should initialize <font SIZE="-1">SDRAM</font> before loading the application.
<dt><b>-micplb</b>
<dd>Assume that ICPLBs are enabled at run time. This has an effect on certain anomaly workarounds. For Linux targets, the default is to assume ICPLBs are enabled; for standalone applications the default is off.</dl>
 

 <i>C6X Options</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-march=</b><i>name</i>
<dd>This specifies the name of the target architecture. <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> uses this name to determine what kind of instructions it can emit when generating assembly code. Permissible names are: <b>c62x</b>, <b>c64x</b>, <b>c64x+</b>, <b>c67x</b>, <b>c67x+</b>, <b>c674x</b>.
<dt><b>-mbig-endian</b>
<dd>Generate code for a big-endian target.
<dt><b>-mlittle-endian</b>
<dd>Generate code for a little-endian target. This is the default.
<dt><b>-msim</b>
<dd>Choose startup files and linker script suitable for the simulator.
<dt><b>-msdata=default</b>
<dd>Put small global and static data in the <tt>&quot;.neardata&quot;</tt> section, which is pointed to by register <tt>&quot;B14&quot;</tt>. Put small uninitialized global and static data in the <tt>&quot;.bss&quot;</tt> section, which is adjacent to the <tt>&quot;.neardata&quot;</tt> section. Put small read-only data into the <tt>&quot;.rodata&quot;</tt> section. The corresponding sections used for large pieces of data are <tt>&quot;.fardata&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;.far&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;.const&quot;</tt>.
<dt><b>-msdata=all</b>
<dd>Put all data, not just small objects, into the sections reserved for small data, and use addressing relative to the <tt>&quot;B14&quot;</tt> register to access them.
<dt><b>-msdata=none</b>
<dd>Make no use of the sections reserved for small data, and use absolute addresses to access all data. Put all initialized global and static data in the <tt>&quot;.fardata&quot;</tt> section, and all uninitialized data in the <tt>&quot;.far&quot;</tt> section. Put all constant data into the <tt>&quot;.const&quot;</tt> section.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>CRIS</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These options are defined specifically for the <font SIZE="-1">CRIS</font> ports.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-march=</b><i>architecture-type</i>
<dd><dt><b>-mcpu=</b><i>architecture-type</i>
<dd>Generate code for the specified architecture. The choices for <i>architecture-type</i> are <b>v3</b>, <b>v8</b> and <b>v10</b> for respectively <font SIZE="-1">ETRAX</font>&nbsp;4, <font SIZE="-1">ETRAX</font>&nbsp;100, and <font SIZE="-1">ETRAX</font>&nbsp;100&nbsp;<font SIZE="-1">LX.</font> Default is <b>v0</b> except for cris-axis-linux-gnu, where the default is <b>v10</b>.
<dt><b>-mtune=</b><i>architecture-type</i>
<dd>Tune to <i>architecture-type</i> everything applicable about the generated code, except for the <font SIZE="-1">ABI</font> and the set of available instructions. The choices for <i>architecture-type</i> are the same as for <b>-march=</b><i>architecture-type</i>.
<dt><b>-mmax-stack-frame=</b><i>n</i>
<dd>Warn when the stack frame of a function exceeds <i>n</i> bytes.
<dt><b>-metrax4</b>
<dd><dt><b>-metrax100</b>
<dd>The options <b>-metrax4</b> and <b>-metrax100</b> are synonyms for <b>-march=v3</b> and <b>-march=v8</b> respectively.
<dt><b>-mmul-bug-workaround</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-mul-bug-workaround</b>
<dd>Work around a bug in the <tt>&quot;muls&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;mulu&quot;</tt> instructions for <font SIZE="-1">CPU</font> models where it applies. This option is active by default.
<dt><b>-mpdebug</b>
<dd>Enable CRIS-specific verbose debug-related information in the assembly code. This option also has the effect of turning off the <b>#NO_APP</b> formatted-code indicator to the assembler at the beginning of the assembly file.
<dt><b>-mcc-init</b>
<dd>Do not use condition-code results from previous instruction; always emit compare and test instructions before use of condition codes.
<dt><b>-mno-side-effects</b>
<dd>Do not emit instructions with side effects in addressing modes other than post-increment.
<dt><b>-mstack-align</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-stack-align</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mdata-align</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-data-align</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mconst-align</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-const-align</b>
<dd>These options (<b>no-</b> options) arrange (eliminate arrangements) for the stack frame, individual data and constants to be aligned for the maximum single data access size for the chosen <font SIZE="-1">CPU</font> model. The default is to arrange for 32-bit alignment. <font SIZE="-1">ABI</font> details such as structure layout are not affected by these options.
<dt><b>-m32-bit</b>
<dd><dt><b>-m16-bit</b>
<dd><dt><b>-m8-bit</b>
<dd>Similar to the stack- data- and const-align options above, these options arrange for stack frame, writable data and constants to all be 32-bit, 16-bit or 8-bit aligned. The default is 32-bit alignment.
<dt><b>-mno-prologue-epilogue</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mprologue-epilogue</b>
<dd>With <b>-mno-prologue-epilogue</b>, the normal function prologue and epilogue which set up the stack frame are omitted and no return instructions or return sequences are generated in the code. Use this option only together with visual inspection of the compiled code: no warnings or errors are generated when call-saved registers must be saved, or storage for local variables needs to be allocated.
<dt><b>-mno-gotplt</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mgotplt</b>
<dd>With <b>-fpic</b> and <b>-fPIC</b>, don't generate (do generate) instruction sequences that load addresses for functions from the <font SIZE="-1">PLT</font> part of the <font SIZE="-1">GOT</font> rather than (traditional on other architectures) calls to the <font SIZE="-1">PLT.</font> The default is <b>-mgotplt</b>.
<dt><b>-melf</b>
<dd>Legacy no-op option only recognized with the cris-axis-elf and cris-axis-linux-gnu targets.
<dt><b>-mlinux</b>
<dd>Legacy no-op option only recognized with the cris-axis-linux-gnu target.
<dt><b>-sim</b>
<dd>This option, recognized for the cris-axis-elf, arranges to link with input-output functions from a simulator library. Code, initialized data and zero-initialized data are allocated consecutively.
<dt><b>-sim2</b>
<dd>Like <b>-sim</b>, but pass linker options to locate initialized data at 0x40000000 and zero-initialized data at 0x80000000.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>CR16</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These options are defined specifically for the <font SIZE="-1">CR16</font> ports.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mmac</b>
<dd>Enable the use of multiply-accumulate instructions. Disabled by default.
<dt><b>-mcr16cplus</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mcr16c</b>
<dd>Generate code for <font SIZE="-1">CR16C</font> or <font SIZE="-1">CR16C+</font> architecture. <font SIZE="-1">CR16C+</font> architecture is default.
<dt><b>-msim</b>
<dd>Links the library libsim.a which is in compatible with simulator. Applicable to <font SIZE="-1">ELF</font> compiler only.
<dt><b>-mint32</b>
<dd>Choose integer type as 32-bit wide.
<dt><b>-mbit-ops</b>
<dd>Generates <tt>&quot;sbit&quot;</tt>/<tt>&quot;cbit&quot;</tt> instructions for bit manipulations.
<dt><b>-mdata-model=</b><i>model</i>
<dd>Choose a data model. The choices for <i>model</i> are <b>near</b>, <b>far</b> or <b>medium</b>. <b>medium</b> is default. However, <b>far</b> is not valid with <b>-mcr16c</b>, as the <font SIZE="-1">CR16C</font> architecture does not support the far data model.</dl>
 

 <i>C-SKY Options</i> 

 <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> supports these options when compiling for C-SKY V2 processors.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-march=</b><i>arch</i>
<dd>Specify the C-SKY target architecture. Valid values for <i>arch</i> are: <b>ck801</b>, <b>ck802</b>, <b>ck803</b>, <b>ck807</b>, and <b>ck810</b>. The default is <b>ck810</b>.
<dt><b>-mcpu=</b><i>cpu</i>
<dd>Specify the C-SKY target processor. Valid values for <i>cpu</i> are: <b>ck801</b>, <b>ck801t</b>, <b>ck802</b>, <b>ck802t</b>, <b>ck802j</b>, <b>ck803</b>, <b>ck803h</b>, <b>ck803t</b>, <b>ck803ht</b>, <b>ck803f</b>, <b>ck803fh</b>, <b>ck803e</b>, <b>ck803eh</b>, <b>ck803et</b>, <b>ck803eht</b>, <b>ck803ef</b>, <b>ck803efh</b>, <b>ck803ft</b>, <b>ck803eft</b>, <b>ck803efht</b>, <b>ck803r1</b>, <b>ck803hr1</b>, <b>ck803tr1</b>, <b>ck803htr1</b>, <b>ck803fr1</b>, <b>ck803fhr1</b>, <b>ck803er1</b>, <b>ck803ehr1</b>, <b>ck803etr1</b>, <b>ck803ehtr1</b>, <b>ck803efr1</b>, <b>ck803efhr1</b>, <b>ck803ftr1</b>, <b>ck803eftr1</b>, <b>ck803efhtr1</b>, <b>ck803s</b>, <b>ck803st</b>, <b>ck803se</b>, <b>ck803sf</b>, <b>ck803sef</b>, <b>ck803seft</b>, <b>ck807e</b>, <b>ck807ef</b>, <b>ck807</b>, <b>ck807f</b>, <b>ck810e</b>, <b>ck810et</b>, <b>ck810ef</b>, <b>ck810eft</b>, <b>ck810</b>, <b>ck810v</b>, <b>ck810f</b>, <b>ck810t</b>, <b>ck810fv</b>, <b>ck810tv</b>, <b>ck810ft</b>, and <b>ck810ftv</b>.
<dt><b>-mbig-endian</b>
<dd><dt><b>-EB</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mlittle-endian</b>
<dd><dt><b>-EL</b>
<dd>Select big- or little-endian code. The default is little-endian.
<dt><b>-mhard-float</b>
<dd><dt><b>-msoft-float</b>
<dd>Select hardware or software floating-point implementations. The default is soft float.
<dt><b>-mdouble-float</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-double-float</b>
<dd>When <b>-mhard-float</b> is in effect, enable generation of double-precision float instructions. This is the default except when compiling for <font SIZE="-1">CK803.</font>
<dt><b>-mfdivdu</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-fdivdu</b>
<dd>When <b>-mhard-float</b> is in effect, enable generation of <tt>&quot;frecipd&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;fsqrtd&quot;</tt>, and <tt>&quot;fdivd&quot;</tt> instructions. This is the default except when compiling for <font SIZE="-1">CK803.</font>
<dt><b>-mfpu=</b><i>fpu</i>
<dd>Select the floating-point processor. This option can only be used with <b>-mhard-float</b>. Values for <i>fpu</i> are <b>fpv2_sf</b> (equivalent to <b>-mno-double-float -mno-fdivdu</b>), <b>fpv2</b> (<b>-mdouble-float -mno-divdu</b>), and <b>fpv2_divd</b> (<b>-mdouble-float -mdivdu</b>).
<dt><b>-melrw</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-elrw</b>
<dd>Enable the extended <tt>&quot;lrw&quot;</tt> instruction. This option defaults to on for <font SIZE="-1">CK801</font> and off otherwise.
<dt><b>-mistack</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-istack</b>
<dd>Enable interrupt stack instructions; the default is off. 

 The <b>-mistack</b> option is required to handle the <tt>&quot;interrupt&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;isr&quot;</tt> function attributes.
<dt><b>-mmp</b>
<dd>Enable multiprocessor instructions; the default is off.
<dt><b>-mcp</b>
<dd>Enable coprocessor instructions; the default is off.
<dt><b>-mcache</b>
<dd>Enable coprocessor instructions; the default is off.
<dt><b>-msecurity</b>
<dd>Enable C-SKY security instructions; the default is off.
<dt><b>-mtrust</b>
<dd>Enable C-SKY trust instructions; the default is off.
<dt><b>-mdsp</b>
<dd><dt><b>-medsp</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mvdsp</b>
<dd>Enable C-SKY <font SIZE="-1">DSP,</font> Enhanced <font SIZE="-1">DSP,</font> or Vector <font SIZE="-1">DSP</font> instructions, respectively. All of these options default to off.
<dt><b>-mdiv</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-div</b>
<dd>Generate divide instructions. Default is off.
<dt><b>-msmart</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-smart</b>
<dd>Generate code for Smart Mode, using only registers numbered 0-7 to allow use of 16-bit instructions. This option is ignored for <font SIZE="-1">CK801</font> where this is the required behavior, and it defaults to on for <font SIZE="-1">CK802.</font> For other targets, the default is off.
<dt><b>-mhigh-registers</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-high-registers</b>
<dd>Generate code using the high registers numbered 16-31. This option is not supported on <font SIZE="-1">CK801, CK802,</font> or <font SIZE="-1">CK803,</font> and is enabled by default for other processors.
<dt><b>-manchor</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-anchor</b>
<dd>Generate code using global anchor symbol addresses.
<dt><b>-mpushpop</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-pushpop</b>
<dd>Generate code using <tt>&quot;push&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;pop&quot;</tt> instructions. This option defaults to on.
<dt><b>-mmultiple-stld</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mstm</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-multiple-stld</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-stm</b>
<dd>Generate code using <tt>&quot;stm&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;ldm&quot;</tt> instructions. This option isn't supported on <font SIZE="-1">CK801</font> but is enabled by default on other processors.
<dt><b>-mconstpool</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-constpool</b>
<dd>Create constant pools in the compiler instead of deferring it to the assembler. This option is the default and required for correct code generation on <font SIZE="-1">CK801</font> and <font SIZE="-1">CK802,</font> and is optional on other processors.
<dt><b>-mstack-size</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-stack-size</b>
<dd>Emit <tt>&quot;.stack_size&quot;</tt> directives for each function in the assembly output. This option defaults to off.
<dt><b>-mccrt</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-ccrt</b>
<dd>Generate code for the C-SKY compiler runtime instead of libgcc. This option defaults to off.
<dt><b>-mbranch-cost=</b><i>n</i>
<dd>Set the branch costs to roughly <tt>&quot;n&quot;</tt> instructions. The default is 1.
<dt><b>-msched-prolog</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-sched-prolog</b>
<dd>Permit scheduling of function prologue and epilogue sequences. Using this option can result in code that is not compliant with the C-SKY V2 <font SIZE="-1">ABI</font> prologue requirements and that cannot be debugged or backtraced. It is disabled by default.</dl>
 

 <i>Darwin Options</i> 

 These options are defined for all architectures running the Darwin operating system. 

 <font SIZE="-1">FSF GCC</font> on Darwin does not create ``fat'' object files; it creates an object file for the single architecture that <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> was built to target. Apple's <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> on Darwin does create ``fat'' files if multiple <b>-arch</b> options are used; it does so by running the compiler or linker multiple times and joining the results together with <i>lipo</i>. 

 The subtype of the file created (like <b>ppc7400</b> or <b>ppc970</b> or <b>i686</b>) is determined by the flags that specify the <font SIZE="-1">ISA</font> that <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> is targeting, like <b>-mcpu</b> or <b>-march</b>. The <b>-force_cpusubtype_ALL</b> option can be used to override this. 

 The Darwin tools vary in their behavior when presented with an <font SIZE="-1">ISA</font> mismatch. The assembler, <i>as</i>, only permits instructions to be used that are valid for the subtype of the file it is generating, so you cannot put 64-bit instructions in a <b>ppc750</b> object file. The linker for shared libraries, <i>/usr/bin/libtool</i>, fails and prints an error if asked to create a shared library with a less restrictive subtype than its input files (for instance, trying to put a <b>ppc970</b> object file in a <b>ppc7400</b> library). The linker for executables, <b>ld</b>, quietly gives the executable the most restrictive subtype of any of its input files.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-F</b><i>dir</i>
<dd>Add the framework directory <i>dir</i> to the head of the list of directories to be searched for header files. These directories are interleaved with those specified by <b>-I</b> options and are scanned in a left-to-right order. 

 A framework directory is a directory with frameworks in it. A framework is a directory with a <i>Headers</i> and/or <i>PrivateHeaders</i> directory contained directly in it that ends in <i>.framework</i>. The name of a framework is the name of this directory excluding the <i>.framework</i>. Headers associated with the framework are found in one of those two directories, with <i>Headers</i> being searched first. A subframework is a framework directory that is in a framework's <i>Frameworks</i> directory. Includes of subframework headers can only appear in a header of a framework that contains the subframework, or in a sibling subframework header. Two subframeworks are siblings if they occur in the same framework. A subframework should not have the same name as a framework; a warning is issued if this is violated. Currently a subframework cannot have subframeworks; in the future, the mechanism may be extended to support this. The standard frameworks can be found in <i>/System/Library/Frameworks</i> and <i>/Library/Frameworks</i>. An example include looks like <tt>&quot;#include &lt;Framework/header.h&gt;&quot;</tt>, where <i>Framework</i> denotes the name of the framework and <i>header.h</i> is found in the <i>PrivateHeaders</i> or <i>Headers</i> directory.
<dt><b>-iframework</b><i>dir</i>
<dd>Like <b>-F</b> except the directory is a treated as a system directory. The main difference between this <b>-iframework</b> and <b>-F</b> is that with <b>-iframework</b> the compiler does not warn about constructs contained within header files found via <i>dir</i>. This option is valid only for the C family of languages.
<dt><b>-gused</b>
<dd>Emit debugging information for symbols that are used. For stabs debugging format, this enables <b>-feliminate-unused-debug-symbols</b>. This is by default <font SIZE="-1">ON.</font>
<dt><b>-gfull</b>
<dd>Emit debugging information for all symbols and types.
<dt><b>-mmacosx-version-min=</b><i>version</i>
<dd>The earliest version of MacOS X that this executable will run on is <i>version</i>. Typical values of <i>version</i> include <tt>10.1</tt>, <tt>10.2</tt>, and <tt>10.3.9</tt>. 

 If the compiler was built to use the system's headers by default, then the default for this option is the system version on which the compiler is running, otherwise the default is to make choices that are compatible with as many systems and code bases as possible.
<dt><b>-mkernel</b>
<dd>Enable kernel development mode. The <b>-mkernel</b> option sets <b>-static</b>, <b>-fno-common</b>, <b>-fno-use-cxa-atexit</b>, <b>-fno-exceptions</b>, <b>-fno-non-call-exceptions</b>, <b>-fapple-kext</b>, <b>-fno-weak</b> and <b>-fno-rtti</b> where applicable. This mode also sets <b>-mno-altivec</b>, <b>-msoft-float</b>, <b>-fno-builtin</b> and <b>-mlong-branch</b> for PowerPC targets.
<dt><b>-mone-byte-bool</b>
<dd>Override the defaults for <tt>&quot;bool&quot;</tt> so that <tt>&quot;sizeof(bool)==1&quot;</tt>. By default <tt>&quot;sizeof(bool)&quot;</tt> is <tt>4</tt> when compiling for Darwin/PowerPC and <tt>1</tt> when compiling for Darwin/x86, so this option has no effect on x86. 

 <b>Warning:</b> The <b>-mone-byte-bool</b> switch causes <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> to generate code that is not binary compatible with code generated without that switch. Using this switch may require recompiling all other modules in a program, including system libraries. Use this switch to conform to a non-default data model.
<dt><b>-mfix-and-continue</b>
<dd><dt><b>-ffix-and-continue</b>
<dd><dt><b>-findirect-data</b>
<dd>Generate code suitable for fast turnaround development, such as to allow <font SIZE="-1">GDB</font> to dynamically load <i>.o</i> files into already-running programs. <b>-findirect-data</b> and <b>-ffix-and-continue</b> are provided for backwards compatibility.
<dt><b>-all_load</b>
<dd>Loads all members of static archive libraries. See man <b><a HREF="/docs/linux/man/1-ld/">ld</a></b>(1) for more information.
<dt><b>-arch_errors_fatal</b>
<dd>Cause the errors having to do with files that have the wrong architecture to be fatal.
<dt><b>-bind_at_load</b>
<dd>Causes the output file to be marked such that the dynamic linker will bind all undefined references when the file is loaded or launched.
<dt><b>-bundle</b>
<dd>Produce a Mach-o bundle format file. See man <b><a HREF="/docs/linux/man/1-ld/">ld</a></b>(1) for more information.
<dt><b>-bundle_loader</b> <i>executable</i>
<dd>This option specifies the <i>executable</i> that will load the build output file being linked. See man <b><a HREF="/docs/linux/man/1-ld/">ld</a></b>(1) for more information.
<dt><b>-dynamiclib</b>
<dd>When passed this option, <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> produces a dynamic library instead of an executable when linking, using the Darwin <i>libtool</i> command.
<dt><b>-force_cpusubtype_ALL</b>
<dd>This causes <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font>'s output file to have the <font SIZE="-1"><b>ALL</b></font> subtype, instead of one controlled by the <b>-mcpu</b> or <b>-march</b> option.
<dt><b>-allowable_client</b> <i>client_name</i>
<dd><dt><b>-client_name</b>
<dd><dt><b>-compatibility_version</b>
<dd><dt><b>-current_version</b>
<dd><dt><b>-dead_strip</b>
<dd><dt><b>-dependency-file</b>
<dd><dt><b>-dylib_file</b>
<dd><dt><b>-dylinker_install_name</b>
<dd><dt><b>-dynamic</b>
<dd><dt><b>-exported_symbols_list</b>
<dd><dt><b>-filelist</b>
<dd><dt><b>-flat_namespace</b>
<dd><dt><b>-force_flat_namespace</b>
<dd><dt><b>-headerpad_max_install_names</b>
<dd><dt><b>-image_base</b>
<dd><dt><b>-init</b>
<dd><dt><b>-install_name</b>
<dd><dt><b>-keep_private_externs</b>
<dd><dt><b>-multi_module</b>
<dd><dt><b>-multiply_defined</b>
<dd><dt><b>-multiply_defined_unused</b>
<dd><dt><b>-noall_load</b>
<dd><dt><b>-no_dead_strip_inits_and_terms</b>
<dd><dt><b>-nofixprebinding</b>
<dd><dt><b>-nomultidefs</b>
<dd><dt><b>-noprebind</b>
<dd><dt><b>-noseglinkedit</b>
<dd><dt><b>-pagezero_size</b>
<dd><dt><b>-prebind</b>
<dd><dt><b>-prebind_all_twolevel_modules</b>
<dd><dt><b>-private_bundle</b>
<dd><dt><b>-read_only_relocs</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sectalign</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sectobjectsymbols</b>
<dd><dt><b>-whyload</b>
<dd><dt><b>-seg1addr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sectcreate</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sectobjectsymbols</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sectorder</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segaddr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segs_read_only_addr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segs_read_write_addr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-seg_addr_table</b>
<dd><dt><b>-seg_addr_table_filename</b>
<dd><dt><b>-seglinkedit</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segprot</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segs_read_only_addr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-segs_read_write_addr</b>
<dd><dt><b>-single_module</b>
<dd><dt><b>-static</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sub_library</b>
<dd><dt><b>-sub_umbrella</b>
<dd><dt><b>-twolevel_namespace</b>
<dd><dt><b>-umbrella</b>
<dd><dt><b>-undefined</b>
<dd><dt><b>-unexported_symbols_list</b>
<dd><dt><b>-weak_reference_mismatches</b>
<dd><dt><b>-whatsloaded</b>
<dd>These options are passed to the Darwin linker. The Darwin linker man page describes them in detail.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>DEC</i></font><i> Alpha Options</i> 

 These <b>-m</b> options are defined for the <font SIZE="-1">DEC</font> Alpha implementations:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mno-soft-float</b>
<dd><dt><b>-msoft-float</b>
<dd>Use (do not use) the hardware floating-point instructions for floating-point operations. When <b>-msoft-float</b> is specified, functions in <i>libgcc.a</i> are used to perform floating-point operations. Unless they are replaced by routines that emulate the floating-point operations, or compiled in such a way as to call such emulations routines, these routines issue floating-point operations. If you are compiling for an Alpha without floating-point operations, you must ensure that the library is built so as not to call them. 

 Note that Alpha implementations without floating-point operations are required to have floating-point registers.
<dt><b>-mfp-reg</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-fp-regs</b>
<dd>Generate code that uses (does not use) the floating-point register set. <b>-mno-fp-regs</b> implies <b>-msoft-float</b>. If the floating-point register set is not used, floating-point operands are passed in integer registers as if they were integers and floating-point results are passed in <tt>$0</tt> instead of <tt>$f0</tt>. This is a non-standard calling sequence, so any function with a floating-point argument or return value called by code compiled with <b>-mno-fp-regs</b> must also be compiled with that option. 

 A typical use of this option is building a kernel that does not use, and hence need not save and restore, any floating-point registers.
<dt><b>-mieee</b>
<dd>The Alpha architecture implements floating-point hardware optimized for maximum performance. It is mostly compliant with the <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> floating-point standard. However, for full compliance, software assistance is required. This option generates code fully IEEE-compliant code <i>except</i> that the <i>inexact-flag</i> is not maintained (see below). If this option is turned on, the preprocessor macro <tt>&quot;_IEEE_FP&quot;</tt> is defined during compilation. The resulting code is less efficient but is able to correctly support denormalized numbers and exceptional <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> values such as not-a-number and plus/minus infinity. Other Alpha compilers call this option <b>-ieee_with_no_inexact</b>.
<dt><b>-mieee-with-inexact</b>
<dd>This is like <b>-mieee</b> except the generated code also maintains the <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> <i>inexact-flag</i>. Turning on this option causes the generated code to implement fully-compliant <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> math. In addition to <tt>&quot;_IEEE_FP&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;_IEEE_FP_EXACT&quot;</tt> is defined as a preprocessor macro. On some Alpha implementations the resulting code may execute significantly slower than the code generated by default. Since there is very little code that depends on the <i>inexact-flag</i>, you should normally not specify this option. Other Alpha compilers call this option <b>-ieee_with_inexact</b>.
<dt><b>-mfp-trap-mode=</b><i>trap-mode</i>
<dd>This option controls what floating-point related traps are enabled. Other Alpha compilers call this option <b>-fptm</b> <i>trap-mode</i>. The trap mode can be set to one of four values:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>n</b>
<dd>This is the default (normal) setting. The only traps that are enabled are the ones that cannot be disabled in software (e.g., division by zero trap).
<dt><b>u</b>
<dd>In addition to the traps enabled by <b>n</b>, underflow traps are enabled as well.
<dt><b>su</b>
<dd>Like <b>u</b>, but the instructions are marked to be safe for software completion (see Alpha architecture manual for details).
<dt><b>sui</b>
<dd>Like <b>su</b>, but inexact traps are enabled as well.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>-mfp-rounding-mode=</b><i>rounding-mode</i>
<dd>Selects the <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> rounding mode. Other Alpha compilers call this option <b>-fprm</b> <i>rounding-mode</i>. The <i>rounding-mode</i> can be one of:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>n</b>
<dd>Normal <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> rounding mode. Floating-point numbers are rounded towards the nearest machine number or towards the even machine number in case of a tie.
<dt><b>m</b>
<dd>Round towards minus infinity.
<dt><b>c</b>
<dd>Chopped rounding mode. Floating-point numbers are rounded towards zero.
<dt><b>d</b>
<dd>Dynamic rounding mode. A field in the floating-point control register (<i>fpcr</i>, see Alpha architecture reference manual) controls the rounding mode in effect. The C library initializes this register for rounding towards plus infinity. Thus, unless your program modifies the <i>fpcr</i>, <b>d</b> corresponds to round towards plus infinity.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>-mtrap-precision=</b><i>trap-precision</i>
<dd>In the Alpha architecture, floating-point traps are imprecise. This means without software assistance it is impossible to recover from a floating trap and program execution normally needs to be terminated. <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> can generate code that can assist operating system trap handlers in determining the exact location that caused a floating-point trap. Depending on the requirements of an application, different levels of precisions can be selected:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>p</b>
<dd>Program precision. This option is the default and means a trap handler can only identify which program caused a floating-point exception.
<dt><b>f</b>
<dd>Function precision. The trap handler can determine the function that caused a floating-point exception.
<dt><b>i</b>
<dd>Instruction precision. The trap handler can determine the exact instruction that caused a floating-point exception.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd>Other Alpha compilers provide the equivalent options called <b>-scope_safe</b> and <b>-resumption_safe</b>.</dl><dt><b>-mieee-conformant</b>
<dd>This option marks the generated code as <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> conformant. You must not use this option unless you also specify <b>-mtrap-precision=i</b> and either <b>-mfp-trap-mode=su</b> or <b>-mfp-trap-mode=sui</b>. Its only effect is to emit the line <b>.eflag 48</b> in the function prologue of the generated assembly file.
<dt><b>-mbuild-constants</b>
<dd>Normally <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> examines a 32- or 64-bit integer constant to see if it can construct it from smaller constants in two or three instructions. If it cannot, it outputs the constant as a literal and generates code to load it from the data segment at run time. 

 Use this option to require <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> to construct <i>all</i> integer constants using code, even if it takes more instructions (the maximum is six). 

 You typically use this option to build a shared library dynamic loader. Itself a shared library, it must relocate itself in memory before it can find the variables and constants in its own data segment.
<dt><b>-mbwx</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-bwx</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mcix</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-cix</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mfix</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-fix</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mmax</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-max</b>
<dd>Indicate whether <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> should generate code to use the optional <font SIZE="-1">BWX, CIX, FIX</font> and <font SIZE="-1">MAX</font> instruction sets. The default is to use the instruction sets supported by the <font SIZE="-1">CPU</font> type specified via <b>-mcpu=</b> option or that of the <font SIZE="-1">CPU</font> on which <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> was built if none is specified.
<dt><b>-mfloat-vax</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mfloat-ieee</b>
<dd>Generate code that uses (does not use) <font SIZE="-1">VAX F</font> and G floating-point arithmetic instead of <font SIZE="-1">IEEE</font> single and double precision.
<dt><b>-mexplicit-relocs</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-explicit-relocs</b>
<dd>Older Alpha assemblers provided no way to generate symbol relocations except via assembler macros. Use of these macros does not allow optimal instruction scheduling. <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> binutils as of version 2.12 supports a new syntax that allows the compiler to explicitly mark which relocations should apply to which instructions. This option is mostly useful for debugging, as <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> detects the capabilities of the assembler when it is built and sets the default accordingly.
<dt><b>-msmall-data</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mlarge-data</b>
<dd>When <b>-mexplicit-relocs</b> is in effect, static data is accessed via <i>gp-relative</i> relocations. When <b>-msmall-data</b> is used, objects 8 bytes long or smaller are placed in a <i>small data area</i> (the <tt>&quot;.sdata&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;.sbss&quot;</tt> sections) and are accessed via 16-bit relocations off of the <tt>$gp</tt> register. This limits the size of the small data area to 64KB, but allows the variables to be directly accessed via a single instruction. 

 The default is <b>-mlarge-data</b>. With this option the data area is limited to just below 2GB. Programs that require more than 2GB of data must use <tt>&quot;malloc&quot;</tt> or <tt>&quot;mmap&quot;</tt> to allocate the data in the heap instead of in the program's data segment. 

 When generating code for shared libraries, <b>-fpic</b> implies <b>-msmall-data</b> and <b>-fPIC</b> implies <b>-mlarge-data</b>.
<dt><b>-msmall-text</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mlarge-text</b>
<dd>When <b>-msmall-text</b> is used, the compiler assumes that the code of the entire program (or shared library) fits in 4MB, and is thus reachable with a branch instruction. When <b>-msmall-data</b> is used, the compiler can assume that all local symbols share the same <tt>$gp</tt> value, and thus reduce the number of instructions required for a function call from 4 to 1. 

 The default is <b>-mlarge-text</b>.
<dt><b>-mcpu=</b><i>cpu_type</i>
<dd>Set the instruction set and instruction scheduling parameters for machine type <i>cpu_type</i>. You can specify either the <font SIZE="-1"><b>EV</b></font> style name or the corresponding chip number. <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> supports scheduling parameters for the <font SIZE="-1">EV4, EV5</font> and <font SIZE="-1">EV6</font> family of processors and chooses the default values for the instruction set from the processor you specify. If you do not specify a processor type, <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> defaults to the processor on which the compiler was built. 

 Supported values for <i>cpu_type</i> are
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>ev4</b>
<dd><dt><b>ev45</b>
<dd><dt><b>21064</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV4</font> and has no instruction set extensions.
<dt><b>ev5</b>
<dd><dt><b>21164</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV5</font> and has no instruction set extensions.
<dt><b>ev56</b>
<dd><dt><b>21164a</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV5</font> and supports the <font SIZE="-1">BWX</font> extension.
<dt><b>pca56</b>
<dd><dt><b>21164pc</b>
<dd><dt><b>21164PC</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV5</font> and supports the <font SIZE="-1">BWX</font> and <font SIZE="-1">MAX</font> extensions.
<dt><b>ev6</b>
<dd><dt><b>21264</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV6</font> and supports the <font SIZE="-1">BWX, FIX,</font> and <font SIZE="-1">MAX</font> extensions.
<dt><b>ev67</b>
<dd><dt><b>21264a</b>
<dd>Schedules as an <font SIZE="-1">EV6</font> and supports the <font SIZE="-1">BWX, CIX, FIX,</font> and <font SIZE="-1">MAX</font> extensions.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd>Native toolchains also support the value <b>native</b>, which selects the best architecture option for the host processor. <b>-mcpu=native</b> has no effect if <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> does not recognize the processor.</dl><dt><b>-mtune=</b><i>cpu_type</i>
<dd>Set only the instruction scheduling parameters for machine type <i>cpu_type</i>. The instruction set is not changed. 

 Native toolchains also support the value <b>native</b>, which selects the best architecture option for the host processor. <b>-mtune=native</b> has no effect if <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> does not recognize the processor.
<dt><b>-mmemory-latency=</b><i>time</i>
<dd>Sets the latency the scheduler should assume for typical memory references as seen by the application. This number is highly dependent on the memory access patterns used by the application and the size of the external cache on the machine. 

 Valid options for <i>time</i> are
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><i>number</i>
<dd>A decimal number representing clock cycles.
<dt><b>L1</b>
<dd><dt><b>L2</b>
<dd><dt><b>L3</b>
<dd><dt><b>main</b>
<dd>The compiler contains estimates of the number of clock cycles for ``typical'' <font SIZE="-1">EV4 &amp; EV5</font> hardware for the Level 1, 2 &amp; 3 caches (also called Dcache, Scache, and Bcache), as well as to main memory. Note that L3 is only valid for <font SIZE="-1">EV5.</font></dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl></dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>FR30</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These options are defined specifically for the <font SIZE="-1">FR30</font> port.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-msmall-model</b>
<dd>Use the small address space model. This can produce smaller code, but it does assume that all symbolic values and addresses fit into a 20-bit range.
<dt><b>-mno-lsim</b>
<dd>Assume that runtime support has been provided and so there is no need to include the simulator library (<i>libsim.a</i>) on the linker command line.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>FT32</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These options are defined specifically for the <font SIZE="-1">FT32</font> port.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-msim</b>
<dd>Specifies that the program will be run on the simulator. This causes an alternate runtime startup and library to be linked. You must not use this option when generating programs that will run on real hardware; you must provide your own runtime library for whatever I/O functions are needed.
<dt><b>-mlra</b>
<dd>Enable Local Register Allocation. This is still experimental for <font SIZE="-1">FT32,</font> so by default the compiler uses standard reload.
<dt><b>-mnodiv</b>
<dd>Do not use div and mod instructions.
<dt><b>-mft32b</b>
<dd>Enable use of the extended instructions of the <font SIZE="-1">FT32B</font> processor.
<dt><b>-mcompress</b>
<dd>Compress all code using the Ft32B code compression scheme.
<dt><b>-mnopm</b>
<dd>Do not generate code that reads program memory.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>FRV</i></font><i> Options</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mgpr-32</b>
<dd>Only use the first 32 general-purpose registers.
<dt><b>-mgpr-64</b>
<dd>Use all 64 general-purpose registers.
<dt><b>-mfpr-32</b>
<dd>Use only the first 32 floating-point registers.
<dt><b>-mfpr-64</b>
<dd>Use all 64 floating-point registers.
<dt><b>-mhard-float</b>
<dd>Use hardware instructions for floating-point operations.
<dt><b>-msoft-float</b>
<dd>Use library routines for floating-point operations.
<dt><b>-malloc-cc</b>
<dd>Dynamically allocate condition code registers.
<dt><b>-mfixed-cc</b>
<dd>Do not try to dynamically allocate condition code registers, only use <tt>&quot;icc0&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;fcc0&quot;</tt>.
<dt><b>-mdword</b>
<dd>Change <font SIZE="-1">ABI</font> to use double word insns.
<dt><b>-mno-dword</b>
<dd>Do not use double word instructions.
<dt><b>-mdouble</b>
<dd>Use floating-point double instructions.
<dt><b>-mno-double</b>
<dd>Do not use floating-point double instructions.
<dt><b>-mmedia</b>
<dd>Use media instructions.
<dt><b>-mno-media</b>
<dd>Do not use media instructions.
<dt><b>-mmuladd</b>
<dd>Use multiply and add/subtract instructions.
<dt><b>-mno-muladd</b>
<dd>Do not use multiply and add/subtract instructions.
<dt><b>-mfdpic</b>
<dd>Select the <font SIZE="-1">FDPIC ABI,</font> which uses function descriptors to represent pointers to functions. Without any PIC/PIE-related options, it implies <b>-fPIE</b>. With <b>-fpic</b> or <b>-fpie</b>, it assumes <font SIZE="-1">GOT</font> entries and small data are within a 12-bit range from the <font SIZE="-1">GOT</font> base address; with <b>-fPIC</b> or <b>-fPIE</b>, <font SIZE="-1">GOT</font> offsets are computed with 32 bits. With a <b>bfin-elf</b> target, this option implies <b>-msim</b>.
<dt><b>-minline-plt</b>
<dd>Enable inlining of <font SIZE="-1">PLT</font> entries in function calls to functions that are not known to bind locally. It has no effect without <b>-mfdpic</b>. It's enabled by default if optimizing for speed and compiling for shared libraries (i.e., <b>-fPIC</b> or <b>-fpic</b>), or when an optimization option such as <b>-O3</b> or above is present in the command line.
<dt><b>-mTLS</b>
<dd>Assume a large <font SIZE="-1">TLS</font> segment when generating thread-local code.
<dt><b>-mtls</b>
<dd>Do not assume a large <font SIZE="-1">TLS</font> segment when generating thread-local code.
<dt><b>-mgprel-ro</b>
<dd>Enable the use of <tt>&quot;GPREL&quot;</tt> relocations in the <font SIZE="-1">FDPIC ABI</font> for data that is known to be in read-only sections. It's enabled by default, except for <b>-fpic</b> or <b>-fpie</b>: even though it may help make the global offset table smaller, it trades 1 instruction for 4. With <b>-fPIC</b> or <b>-fPIE</b>, it trades 3 instructions for 4, one of which may be shared by multiple symbols, and it avoids the need for a <font SIZE="-1">GOT</font> entry for the referenced symbol, so it's more likely to be a win. If it is not, <b>-mno-gprel-ro</b> can be used to disable it.
<dt><b>-multilib-library-pic</b>
<dd>Link with the (library, not <font SIZE="-1">FD</font>) pic libraries. It's implied by <b>-mlibrary-pic</b>, as well as by <b>-fPIC</b> and <b>-fpic</b> without <b>-mfdpic</b>. You should never have to use it explicitly.
<dt><b>-mlinked-fp</b>
<dd>Follow the <font SIZE="-1">EABI</font> requirement of always creating a frame pointer whenever a stack frame is allocated. This option is enabled by default and can be disabled with <b>-mno-linked-fp</b>.
<dt><b>-mlong-calls</b>
<dd>Use indirect addressing to call functions outside the current compilation unit. This allows the functions to be placed anywhere within the 32-bit address space.
<dt><b>-malign-labels</b>
<dd>Try to align labels to an 8-byte boundary by inserting NOPs into the previous packet. This option only has an effect when <font SIZE="-1">VLIW</font> packing is enabled. It doesn't create new packets; it merely adds NOPs to existing ones.
<dt><b>-mlibrary-pic</b>
<dd>Generate position-independent <font SIZE="-1">EABI</font> code.
<dt><b>-macc-4</b>
<dd>Use only the first four media accumulator registers.
<dt><b>-macc-8</b>
<dd>Use all eight media accumulator registers.
<dt><b>-mpack</b>
<dd>Pack <font SIZE="-1">VLIW</font> instructions.
<dt><b>-mno-pack</b>
<dd>Do not pack <font SIZE="-1">VLIW</font> instructions.
<dt><b>-mno-eflags</b>
<dd>Do not mark <font SIZE="-1">ABI</font> switches in e_flags.
<dt><b>-mcond-move</b>
<dd>Enable the use of conditional-move instructions (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-cond-move</b>
<dd>Disable the use of conditional-move instructions. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mscc</b>
<dd>Enable the use of conditional set instructions (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-scc</b>
<dd>Disable the use of conditional set instructions. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mcond-exec</b>
<dd>Enable the use of conditional execution (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-cond-exec</b>
<dd>Disable the use of conditional execution. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mvliw-branch</b>
<dd>Run a pass to pack branches into <font SIZE="-1">VLIW</font> instructions (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-vliw-branch</b>
<dd>Do not run a pass to pack branches into <font SIZE="-1">VLIW</font> instructions. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mmulti-cond-exec</b>
<dd>Enable optimization of <tt>&quot;&amp;&amp;&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;||&quot;</tt> in conditional execution (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-multi-cond-exec</b>
<dd>Disable optimization of <tt>&quot;&amp;&amp;&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;||&quot;</tt> in conditional execution. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mnested-cond-exec</b>
<dd>Enable nested conditional execution optimizations (default). 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-mno-nested-cond-exec</b>
<dd>Disable nested conditional execution optimizations. 

 This switch is mainly for debugging the compiler and will likely be removed in a future version.
<dt><b>-moptimize-membar</b>
<dd>This switch removes redundant <tt>&quot;membar&quot;</tt> instructions from the compiler-generated code. It is enabled by default.
<dt><b>-mno-optimize-membar</b>
<dd>This switch disables the automatic removal of redundant <tt>&quot;membar&quot;</tt> instructions from the generated code.
<dt><b>-mtomcat-stats</b>
<dd>Cause gas to print out tomcat statistics.
<dt><b>-mcpu=</b><i>cpu</i>
<dd>Select the processor type for which to generate code. Possible values are <b>frv</b>, <b>fr550</b>, <b>tomcat</b>, <b>fr500</b>, <b>fr450</b>, <b>fr405</b>, <b>fr400</b>, <b>fr300</b> and <b>simple</b>.</dl>
 

 <i>GNU/Linux Options</i> 

 These <b>-m</b> options are defined for GNU/Linux targets:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mglibc</b>
<dd>Use the <font SIZE="-1">GNU C</font> library. This is the default except on <b>*-*-linux-*uclibc*</b>, <b>*-*-linux-*musl*</b> and <b>*-*-linux-*android*</b> targets.
<dt><b>-muclibc</b>
<dd>Use uClibc C library. This is the default on <b>*-*-linux-*uclibc*</b> targets.
<dt><b>-mmusl</b>
<dd>Use the musl C library. This is the default on <b>*-*-linux-*musl*</b> targets.
<dt><b>-mbionic</b>
<dd>Use Bionic C library. This is the default on <b>*-*-linux-*android*</b> targets.
<dt><b>-mandroid</b>
<dd>Compile code compatible with Android platform. This is the default on <b>*-*-linux-*android*</b> targets. 

 When compiling, this option enables <b>-mbionic</b>, <b>-fPIC</b>, <b>-fno-exceptions</b> and <b>-fno-rtti</b> by default. When linking, this option makes the <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> driver pass Android-specific options to the linker. Finally, this option causes the preprocessor macro <tt>&quot;__ANDROID__&quot;</tt> to be defined.
<dt><b>-tno-android-cc</b>
<dd>Disable compilation effects of <b>-mandroid</b>, i.e., do not enable <b>-mbionic</b>, <b>-fPIC</b>, <b>-fno-exceptions</b> and <b>-fno-rtti</b> by default.
<dt><b>-tno-android-ld</b>
<dd>Disable linking effects of <b>-mandroid</b>, i.e., pass standard Linux linking options to the linker.</dl>
 

 <i>H8/300 Options</i> 

 These <b>-m</b> options are defined for the H8/300 implementations:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mrelax</b>
<dd>Shorten some address references at link time, when possible; uses the linker option <b>-relax</b>.
<dt><b>-mh</b>
<dd>Generate code for the H8/300H.
<dt><b>-ms</b>
<dd>Generate code for the H8S.
<dt><b>-mn</b>
<dd>Generate code for the H8S and H8/300H in the normal mode. This switch must be used either with <b>-mh</b> or <b>-ms</b>.
<dt><b>-ms2600</b>
<dd>Generate code for the H8S/2600. This switch must be used with <b>-ms</b>.
<dt><b>-mexr</b>
<dd>Extended registers are stored on stack before execution of function with monitor attribute. Default option is <b>-mexr</b>. This option is valid only for H8S targets.
<dt><b>-mno-exr</b>
<dd>Extended registers are not stored on stack before execution of function with monitor attribute. Default option is <b>-mno-exr</b>. This option is valid only for H8S targets.
<dt><b>-mint32</b>
<dd>Make <tt>&quot;int&quot;</tt> data 32 bits by default.
<dt><b>-malign-300</b>
<dd>On the H8/300H and H8S, use the same alignment rules as for the H8/300. The default for the H8/300H and H8S is to align longs and floats on 4-byte boundaries. <b>-malign-300</b> causes them to be aligned on 2-byte boundaries. This option has no effect on the H8/300.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>HPPA</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These <b>-m</b> options are defined for the <font SIZE="-1">HPPA</font> family of computers:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-march=</b><i>architecture-type</i>
<dd>Generate code for the specified architecture. The choices for <i>architecture-type</i> are <b>1.0</b> for <font SIZE="-1">PA 1.0,</font> <b>1.1</b> for <font SIZE="-1">PA 1.1,</font> and <b>2.0</b> for <font SIZE="-1">PA 2.0</font> processors. Refer to <i>/usr/lib/sched.models</i> on an HP-UX system to determine the proper architecture option for your machine. Code compiled for lower numbered architectures runs on higher numbered architectures, but not the other way around.
<dt><b>-mpa-risc-1-0</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mpa-risc-1-1</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mpa-risc-2-0</b>
<dd>Synonyms for <b>-march=1.0</b>, <b>-march=1.1</b>, and <b>-march=2.0</b> respectively.
<dt><b>-mcaller-copies</b>
<dd>The caller copies function arguments passed by hidden reference. This option should be used with care as it is not compatible with the default 32-bit runtime. However, only aggregates larger than eight bytes are passed by hidden reference and the option provides better compatibility with OpenMP.
<dt><b>-mjump-in-delay</b>
<dd>This option is ignored and provided for compatibility purposes only.
<dt><b>-mdisable-fpregs</b>
<dd>Prevent floating-point registers from being used in any manner. This is necessary for compiling kernels that perform lazy context switching of floating-point registers. If you use this option and attempt to perform floating-point operations, the compiler aborts.
<dt><b>-mdisable-indexing</b>
<dd>Prevent the compiler from using indexing address modes. This avoids some rather obscure problems when compiling <font SIZE="-1">MIG</font> generated code under <font SIZE="-1">MACH.</font>
<dt><b>-mno-space-regs</b>
<dd>Generate code that assumes the target has no space registers. This allows <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> to generate faster indirect calls and use unscaled index address modes. 

 Such code is suitable for level 0 <font SIZE="-1">PA</font> systems and kernels.
<dt><b>-mfast-indirect-calls</b>
<dd>Generate code that assumes calls never cross space boundaries. This allows <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> to emit code that performs faster indirect calls. 

 This option does not work in the presence of shared libraries or nested functions.
<dt><b>-mfixed-range=</b><i>register-range</i>
<dd>Generate code treating the given register range as fixed registers. A fixed register is one that the register allocator cannot use. This is useful when compiling kernel code. A register range is specified as two registers separated by a dash. Multiple register ranges can be specified separated by a comma.
<dt><b>-mlong-load-store</b>
<dd>Generate 3-instruction load and store sequences as sometimes required by the HP-UX 10 linker. This is equivalent to the <b>+k</b> option to the <font SIZE="-1">HP</font> compilers.
<dt><b>-mportable-runtime</b>
<dd>Use the portable calling conventions proposed by <font SIZE="-1">HP</font> for <font SIZE="-1">ELF</font> systems.
<dt><b>-mgas</b>
<dd>Enable the use of assembler directives only <font SIZE="-1">GAS</font> understands.
<dt><b>-mschedule=</b><i>cpu-type</i>
<dd>Schedule code according to the constraints for the machine type <i>cpu-type</i>. The choices for <i>cpu-type</i> are <b>700</b> <b>7100</b>, <b>7100LC</b>, <b>7200</b>, <b>7300</b> and <b>8000</b>. Refer to <i>/usr/lib/sched.models</i> on an HP-UX system to determine the proper scheduling option for your machine. The default scheduling is <b>8000</b>.
<dt><b>-mlinker-opt</b>
<dd>Enable the optimization pass in the HP-UX linker. Note this makes symbolic debugging impossible. It also triggers a bug in the HP-UX 8 and HP-UX 9 linkers in which they give bogus error messages when linking some programs.
<dt><b>-msoft-float</b>
<dd>Generate output containing library calls for floating point. <b>Warning:</b> the requisite libraries are not available for all <font SIZE="-1">HPPA</font> targets. Normally the facilities of the machine's usual C compiler are used, but this cannot be done directly in cross-compilation. You must make your own arrangements to provide suitable library functions for cross-compilation. 

 <b>-msoft-float</b> changes the calling convention in the output file; therefore, it is only useful if you compile <i>all</i> of a program with this option. In particular, you need to compile <i>libgcc.a</i>, the library that comes with <font SIZE="-1">GCC,</font> with <b>-msoft-float</b> in order for this to work.
<dt><b>-msio</b>
<dd>Generate the predefine, <tt>&quot;_SIO&quot;</tt>, for server <font SIZE="-1">IO.</font> The default is <b>-mwsio</b>. This generates the predefines, <tt>&quot;__hp9000s700&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;__hp9000s700__&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;_WSIO&quot;</tt>, for workstation <font SIZE="-1">IO.</font> These options are available under HP-UX and HI-UX.
<dt><b>-mgnu-ld</b>
<dd>Use options specific to <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> <b>ld</b>. This passes <b>-shared</b> to <b>ld</b> when building a shared library. It is the default when <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> is configured, explicitly or implicitly, with the <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> linker. This option does not affect which <b>ld</b> is called; it only changes what parameters are passed to that <b>ld</b>. The <b>ld</b> that is called is determined by the <b>--with-ld</b> configure option, <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font>'s program search path, and finally by the user's <font SIZE="-1"><b>PATH</b></font>. The linker used by <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> can be printed using <b>which `gcc -print-prog-name=ld`</b>. This option is only available on the 64-bit HP-UX <font SIZE="-1">GCC,</font> i.e. configured with <b>hppa*64*-*-hpux*</b>.
<dt><b>-mhp-ld</b>
<dd>Use options specific to <font SIZE="-1">HP</font> <b>ld</b>. This passes <b>-b</b> to <b>ld</b> when building a shared library and passes <b>+Accept TypeMismatch</b> to <b>ld</b> on all links. It is the default when <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> is configured, explicitly or implicitly, with the <font SIZE="-1">HP</font> linker. This option does not affect which <b>ld</b> is called; it only changes what parameters are passed to that <b>ld</b>. The <b>ld</b> that is called is determined by the <b>--with-ld</b> configure option, <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font>'s program search path, and finally by the user's <font SIZE="-1"><b>PATH</b></font>. The linker used by <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> can be printed using <b>which `gcc -print-prog-name=ld`</b>. This option is only available on the 64-bit HP-UX <font SIZE="-1">GCC,</font> i.e. configured with <b>hppa*64*-*-hpux*</b>.
<dt><b>-mlong-calls</b>
<dd>Generate code that uses long call sequences. This ensures that a call is always able to reach linker generated stubs. The default is to generate long calls only when the distance from the call site to the beginning of the function or translation unit, as the case may be, exceeds a predefined limit set by the branch type being used. The limits for normal calls are 7,600,000 and 240,000 bytes, respectively for the <font SIZE="-1">PA 2.0</font> and <font SIZE="-1">PA 1.X</font> architectures. Sibcalls are always limited at 240,000 bytes. 

 Distances are measured from the beginning of functions when using the <b>-ffunction-sections</b> option, or when using the <b>-mgas</b> and <b>-mno-portable-runtime</b> options together under HP-UX with the <font SIZE="-1">SOM</font> linker. 

 It is normally not desirable to use this option as it degrades performance. However, it may be useful in large applications, particularly when partial linking is used to build the application. 

 The types of long calls used depends on the capabilities of the assembler and linker, and the type of code being generated. The impact on systems that support long absolute calls, and long pic symbol-difference or pc-relative calls should be relatively small. However, an indirect call is used on 32-bit <font SIZE="-1">ELF</font> systems in pic code and it is quite long.
<dt><b>-munix=</b><i>unix-std</i>
<dd>Generate compiler predefines and select a startfile for the specified <font SIZE="-1">UNIX</font> standard. The choices for <i>unix-std</i> are <b>93</b>, <b>95</b> and <b>98</b>. <b>93</b> is supported on all HP-UX versions. <b>95</b> is available on HP-UX 10.10 and later. <b>98</b> is available on HP-UX 11.11 and later. The default values are <b>93</b> for HP-UX 10.00, <b>95</b> for HP-UX 10.10 though to 11.00, and <b>98</b> for HP-UX 11.11 and later. 

 <b>-munix=93</b> provides the same predefines as <font SIZE="-1">GCC 3.3</font> and 3.4. <b>-munix=95</b> provides additional predefines for <tt>&quot;XOPEN_UNIX&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;_XOPEN_SOURCE_EXTENDED&quot;</tt>, and the startfile <i>unix95.o</i>. <b>-munix=98</b> provides additional predefines for <tt>&quot;_XOPEN_UNIX&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;_XOPEN_SOURCE_EXTENDED&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;_INCLUDE__STDC_A1_SOURCE&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;_INCLUDE_XOPEN_SOURCE_500&quot;</tt>, and the startfile <i>unix98.o</i>. 

 It is <i>important</i> to note that this option changes the interfaces for various library routines. It also affects the operational behavior of the C library. Thus, <i>extreme</i> care is needed in using this option. 

 Library code that is intended to operate with more than one <font SIZE="-1">UNIX</font> standard must test, set and restore the variable <tt>&quot;__xpg4_extended_mask&quot;</tt> as appropriate. Most <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> software doesn't provide this capability.
<dt><b>-nolibdld</b>
<dd>Suppress the generation of link options to search libdld.sl when the <b>-static</b> option is specified on HP-UX 10 and later.
<dt><b>-static</b>
<dd>The HP-UX implementation of setlocale in libc has a dependency on libdld.sl. There isn't an archive version of libdld.sl. Thus, when the <b>-static</b> option is specified, special link options are needed to resolve this dependency. 

 On HP-UX 10 and later, the <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> driver adds the necessary options to link with libdld.sl when the <b>-static</b> option is specified. This causes the resulting binary to be dynamic. On the 64-bit port, the linkers generate dynamic binaries by default in any case. The <b>-nolibdld</b> option can be used to prevent the <font SIZE="-1">GCC</font> driver from adding these link options.
<dt><b>-threads</b>
<dd>Add support for multithreading with the <i>dce thread</i> library under HP-UX. This option sets flags for both the preprocessor and linker.</dl>
 

 <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>IA-64</i></font><i> Options</i> 

 These are the <b>-m</b> options defined for the Intel <font SIZE="-1">IA-64</font> architecture.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-mbig-endian</b>
<dd>Generate code for a big-endian target. This is the default for HP-UX.
<dt><b>-mlittle-endian</b>
<dd>Generate code for a little-endian target. This is the default for <font SIZE="-1">AIX5</font> and GNU/Linux.
<dt><b>-mgnu-as</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-gnu-as</b>
<dd>Generate (or don't) code for the <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> assembler. This is the default.
<dt><b>-mgnu-ld</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-gnu-ld</b>
<dd>Generate (or don't) code for the <font SIZE="-1">GNU</font> linker. This is the default.
<dt><b>-mno-pic</b>
<dd>Generate code that does not use a global pointer register. The result is not position independent code, and violates the <font SIZE="-1">IA-64 ABI.</font>
<dt><b>-mvolatile-asm-stop</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-volatile-asm-stop</b>
<dd>Generate (or don't) a stop bit immediately before and after volatile asm statements.
<dt><b>-mregister-names</b>
<dd><dt><b>-mno-register-names</b>
<dd>Generate (or don't) <b>in</b>, <b>loc</b>, and <b>out</b> register names for the stacked registers. This may make assembler output more readable.
<dt><b>-mno-sdata</b>
<dd><dt><b>-msdata</b>
<dd>Disable (or enable) optimizations that use the small data section. This may be useful for working around optimizer bugs.
<dt><b>-mconstant-gp</b>
<dd>Generate code that uses a single constant global pointer value. This is useful when compiling kernel code.
<dt><b>-mauto-pic</b>
<dd>Generate code that is self-relocatable. This implies <b>-mconstant-gp</b>. This is useful when compiling firmware code.
<dt><b>-minline-float-divide-min-latency</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline divides of floating-point values using the minimum latency algorithm.
<dt><b>-minline-float-divide-max-throughput</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline divides of floating-point values using the maximum throughput algorithm.
<dt><b>-mno-inline-float-divide</b>
<dd>Do not generate inline code for divides of floating-point values.
<dt><b>-minline-int-divide-min-latency</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline divides of integer values using the minimum latency algorithm.
<dt><b>-minline-int-divide-max-throughput</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline divides of integer values using the maximum throughput algorithm.
<dt><b>-mno-inline-int-divide</b>
<dd>Do not generate inline code for divides of integer values.
<dt><b>-minline-sqrt-min-latency</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline square roots using the minimum latency algorithm.
<dt><b>-minline-sqrt-max-throughput</b>
<dd>Generate code for inline square roots using the maximum throughput algorithm.
<dt><b>-mno-inline-sqrt</b>
<dd>Do not generate inline code for <tt>&quot;sqrt&quot;</tt>.
<dt><b>-mfused-madd</b>
